name: Ājīvika
info: The Ājīvikas were an ancient Indian school of renunciates, a Śramaṇa movement known for the doctrine of niyati, absolute fate, and for denying free will; it arose about the 5th century BCE and survived in southern India into the 14th century CE.

facts.origin: northern India, generally held to be in the 5th century BCE, though the exact origins are unknown; Buddhist and Jain texts name Savatthi (Śrāvastī) as the hub of the Ājīvikas
facts.founder: Makkhali Gosala (Sanskrit Gośala Maskariputra, c. 484 BCE) is generally considered the founder; some sources call him only the leader of a large congregation, and Jarl Charpentier and others suggest the tradition is older
facts.scriptures: lost: the primary texts are said to have included the ten Purvas (eight Mahanimittas and two Maggas) and the Onpatu Katir, but the movement is known only from the writings of Buddhists, Jains and others
facts.followers: none: the last dated inscription that mentions a tax on Ājīvikas is of 1346 CE, and stray references to survivors run to the 15th century

t: The Ājīvikas taught niyati, absolute determinism: everything that has happened, is happening and will happen is preordained by cosmic principles, there is no free will, and the karma doctrine is a fallacy.
Their own scriptures are lost, so everything known of them comes from Buddhist, Jain and other texts, written largely by rivals, and scholars question how fairly these describe them.

Ashoka's inscriptions in the Barabar Caves in Bihar, the oldest surviving cave temples of ancient India, record his gifts to the Ājīvikas; tax inscriptions show the school in southern India until 1346.
dyk: In several Barabar Cave inscriptions the word “Ājīvikas” was later chiselled out, probably by religious rivals while the Brahmi script was still understood; the original lettering is so deep that it can still be read.
ev: Makkhali Gosala, generally considered the founder of the Ājīvikas, lives as a contemporary of the Buddha and Mahavira
Ashoka dedicates Barabar Caves to the Ājīvikas in the 12th year of his reign; further dedications follow in his 19th year, about 251 BCE
After the decline of the Maurya Empire the Ājīvikas find only occasional mention in Sanskrit literature
The Pallava king Simhavarman II is the earliest ruler of a series of southern Indian inscriptions that record a tax on Ājīvikas
Varahamihira's Brhaj-jataka mentions the Ājīvikas among the major ascetic groups
The Jain commentator Mallisena, writing the Syadvada-manjari, suggests that the Ājīvikas still existed in his time
The last dated inscription recording a tax on Ājīvikas or Acuvas is set up near Kolar

sections.origins:
Buddhist and Jain texts name Makkhali Gosala (Sanskrit Gośala Maskariputra) as a contemporary of the Buddha and Mahavira, and the Ājīvikas are generally held to have begun in the 5th century BCE, although their exact origins are unknown. In the Sandaka Sutta they are said to recognise three emancipators: Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca and Makkhali Gosāla. Gosala is generally considered the founder of the movement, but some sources state that he led a large congregation of ascetics without founding it, and Jarl Charpentier and others suggest that the tradition existed well before his birth.

The Jain Bhagavati Sutra relates that he was born at Saravana, near Savatthi, to Mankha, a professional mendicant, and his mother Bhaddā; his name Gosala means “cowshed” and refers to his humble birthplace. According to the same text he was for six years a disciple of Mahavira, after which the two quarrelled and parted. Gosala argued that the Gosala who had been Mahavira's companion had died and that a different soul now inhabited his body, which Mahavira called sophistry. The Bhagavati Sutra also mentions a debate and then “coming to blows” between the two factions.
sections.beliefs:
The distinctive doctrine of the Ājīvikas was niyati, “fate”. According to Jain and Buddhist texts they held that everything in human life and the universe is preordained by cosmic principles, that true choice does not exist, and that religious or ethical practice therefore has no effect on one's future. They regarded the karma theory as a fallacy. James Lochtefeld compares the universe to a ball of wrapped string that unrolls until it is done and then goes no further. Riepe notes that this did not make them pessimists: as with Calvinists in Europe, he calls them optimists. Makkhali Gosala seems to have combined niyati with svabhava (nature) and sangati (change), and one reading holds that he thought some future events, such as salvation for all, to be strictly determined.

The Ājīvikas were considered atheists and presumed no creator deity. They held that every being has a soul (ātman), which passes through many births and progresses towards its predestined nirvana, and that the soul has a material form. Their atomism held that all things are made of atoms whose aggregation is governed by cosmic rules. Buddhist texts report an antinomian ethics, that there are no objective moral laws, yet both Jain and Buddhist records say the Ājīvikas lived a simple ascetic life without clothes or possessions. Tamil literature suggests they practised non-violence and vegetarianism.
sections.texts:
The Ājīvikas are said to have had a fully elaborate philosophy produced by their scholars and logicians, but those texts are lost, and the original scriptures are probably gone. The primary texts are said to have included the ten Purvas (eight Mahanimittas and two Maggas) and the Onpatu Katir. The Mahanimittas claim that the Bhagavati Sutra was drawn from the teachings Gosala received from Mahavira when he was his disciple, and they gave long sections to mapping the sun, moon, planets and stars and to astrology and fortune telling.

What is known comes from secondary sources: inconsistent fragments in Jain texts such as the Bhagavati Sutra, in Buddhist texts such as the Samaññaphala Sutta, the Sandaka Sutta and Buddhaghosa's commentary on the first of these, and a few mentions in Hindu texts such as the Vayu Purana. Later Tamil works, the Nīlakēci and the Manimekalai among them, also describe Ājīvika views; the Nīlakēci tells of two divinities, Okkali and Ōkali, who instructed men in the scriptures, and three Tamil texts list seven kayas, elements of earth, water, fire, air, joy, sorrow and life. Because these accounts were written by rivals, scholars question whether the school has been fairly summarised, and some suspect deliberate distortion. Paul Dundas doubts that a doctrine denying the efficacy of effort could have grounded a path of renunciation. Johannes Bronkhorst argues that Gosala taught that ascetic practice can stop new karma but not remove old karma.
sections.spread:
Buddhist and Jain texts name the city of Savatthi (Śrāvastī), near Ayodhya in what is now Uttar Pradesh, as the hub of the Ājīvikas in the 1st millennium BCE. The school spread rapidly across ancient South Asia, with a Sangha Geham, a community centre, on the island now called Sri Lanka and a presence in the western state of Gujarat by the 4th century BCE, in the age of the Maurya Empire. The Ashokavadana, a legend of the 4th century CE, says that the emperor Bindusara and his chief queen Shubhadrangi followed this philosophy, and the school is held to have reached its peak of popularity in his reign.

After the decline of the Maurya Empire in the 2nd century BCE the Ājīvikas find only occasional mention in Sanskrit literature. In northern India they may have become insignificant by the Shunga period, and references in the Vayu Purana suggest that during the Gupta period their practices had changed substantially and the sect was declining rapidly. They continued in the south: at least 17 inscriptions from southern India, from the time of the Pallava king Simhavarman II (c. 446 CE) to the 14th century, record a tax on Ājīvikas or Acuvas, believed to be a Tamil form of the name; the last, of 1346 CE, were found at three places around Kolar. Inscriptions suggest a significant presence in Karnataka, especially in Kolar district, and in parts of Tamil Nadu. A. L. Basham thinks they may have survived there until the 15th century; the 14th-century Sarva-Darshana-Sangraha does not mention them.
sections.community:
The Ājīvikas were organised renunciates who formed discrete communities, though the precise identity of the Ājīvikas and their relationships with other movements are not well understood. The school and the Cārvāka philosophy appealed most to the warrior, industrial and mercantile classes of ancient Indian society. Scholars classify them differently: Riepe calls them a distinct heterodox school, Raju says that Ājīvikas and Cārvākas can be called Hindus, and Ashoka's inscriptions suggest that he considered them more closely related to the Vedic schools than to Buddhists or Jains.

The Barabar Caves in Jehanabad district, Bihar, are the oldest surviving cave temples of ancient India. Their dedications to the Ājīvikas were engraved in the 12th and 19th years of Ashoka's reign, about 258 and 251 BCE. Each cave has a large rectangular hall and a small circular domed chamber, and they were probably used for meditation. The Ashokavadana says that Ashoka, after turning to Buddhism, ordered the killing of all Ājīvikas in Pundravardhana and that about 18,000 were supposedly executed; the whole story may be apocryphal, and K. T. S. Sarao and Benimadhab Barua call stories of such persecution a fabrication born of sectarian propaganda, since his own inscriptions record generous gifts to the Ājīvikas. Basham holds that any ruler of Magadha between the Maurya and Gupta periods may have persecuted them.
sections.legacy:
Several writers suggest that the Ājīvikas influenced other schools. Isaeva suggests that their ideas affected Buddhism and various Vedic schools, and Riepe holds that the details of their atomism gave the foundations of later atomist theories in the Jain, Buddhist and Vedic traditions. The Jains, whose atomic theory was closest to theirs, began to claim to have first formulated an Indian atomism only with the later Avisakya Sūtra, and Basham regards the Vaiśeṣika atomism as different from theirs and more complete. Basham also proposes that they may have influenced Dvaita Vedanta.

The Ājīvikas seem to have faded rather than disappeared at a stroke. Basham notes several cases in which other writers confuse them with other groups: a commentator of the Achara-sara takes them for Buddhists, and in the Neelakesi their leader asks that his followers not be mistaken for Digambaras. He concludes that the surviving Ājīvikas may have adopted some beliefs and customs of the more popular faiths and possibly merged with them, and that growing Hindu, Buddhist and Jain influence may have led to their decline. The Barabar Caves were later occupied by Buddhists, Hindus and Muslims, and their carved dedications, with the word Ājīvikas defaced in some places, are the most visible trace of the school.

summary: The Ājīvikas were an ancient Indian renunciant movement, traditionally founded by Makkhali Gosala in the 5th century BCE, that taught absolute fate and rejected karma. Known only through the texts of Buddhist, Jain and other writers, who were often rivals, they enjoyed Mauryan patronage and survived in southern India until inscriptions of the 14th century.
notes: Dates: start -500 circa ('generally accepted to be the 5th century BCE'; Gosala 'c. 484 BCE'). Event 'c. 484 BCE' uses the article's Gosala date. End 1346 circa: last dated tax inscription; the article also says Basham thinks they survived to the 15th century, and the intro says 'nearly 2,000 years through the 13th and 14th centuries'. Hultzsch and Hoernlé think Acuva means Jains, Chakravarti doubts the equivalence; I report Acuva as 'believed to be' a Tamil form, as the article does.

Contradictions left out: the lede puts the peak 'during the rule of Bindusara, around the 4th century BCE' while the article elsewhere puts the peak in the late 1st millennium BCE and Maurya Bindusara is 3rd century BCE; I give only 'in his reign' per the Ashokavadana. The lede says Ājīvikas 'mostly considered atheists' yet a Tamil text has two divinities; both reported. The article gives the 15th century survival as well as 14th; the Hindu texts' date for Ājīvika 'sect' decline (Vayu Purana, Gupta period).

Left out for length: the Varahamihira/Utpala dispute, Hultzsch's and Banerji Sastri's theories on the defacement of the caves, Kharavela, the sesame-plant argument details beyond the summary, Isaeva's name beyond the one mention.
The 'Ashoka dedications' event: the article gives the 12th year as about 258 BCE and the 19th as 251 BCE on a coronation date of 269 BCE; it also gives r. 273-232 BCE. I did not choose between them.
Event c. 446 is the earliest of the inscriptions the article dates; the article says the inscriptions 'range from the time of' Simhavarman II (c. 446 CE).

Faith map coordinates are general geography (Savatthi, Barabar, Kolar, Anuradhapura region for Sri Lanka, Gujarat). Sri Lanka and Gujarat start 300 BCE: the article says 'by the 4th century BCE', which I read as -350, then use -350. Savatthi hub: no date more precise than the 1st millennium BCE.
References left empty for the editor; the article's reference list names Basham (1951), Balcerowicz (2015), Jayatilleke (1963) and Warder (1998).
